articles.title: Not Before Us: The Federal Circuit Sidesteps Schedule A in Jacki Easlick
articles.content:
联邦巡回法院维持了杰基·伊斯利克公司（Jacki Easlick, LLC）诉CJ Emerald公司（CJ Emerald）的设计专利案件中拒绝发布临时禁令的裁决（案号：2024-1538，-1826，2026年8月14日）。该案涉及所谓的“Schedule A”设计专利案件，我曾于6月在Range of Motion全庭重审请愿书仍在审理期间讨论过该案。目前这两起案件均已结案。

本次判决书内容较为简洁，就像该案涉案的手袋挂钩一样轻量。该判决是非建立先例性的，基本上认为原审法院的裁决没有滥用自由裁量权。更有趣的是，该判决书提出了一些问题，但拒绝直接回答。

值得一提的是，判决书将大学教授提交的友情陈述书描述为“认为所谓的‘Schedule A’案件在法律上是允许的”，这似乎是一个重大笔误，因为友情陈述书实际上主张相反的观点，即这些案件在法律上是不允许的。

杰基·伊斯利克公司拥有美国设计专利号D695,526，专利名为“TOTE HANGER”，这是一种由两部分组成的挂钩，可让手袋与衣柜横杆垂直悬挂。这种产品很容易在亚马逊或其他在线商店被复制和出售。2023年，伊斯利克公司在宾夕法尼亚州西区联邦法院对67名在线卖家提起诉讼，并当天获得了针对所有被告的单方临时禁令，包括资产冻结令。其中一名被告AccEncyc是一家中国的亚马逊卖家，出庭并对侵权提出异议。地区法院在“成功可能性”和“不可弥补的损害”两个方面均拒绝了临时禁令。伊斯利克公司申请再审，并提供了之前未提交的实体挂钩。法院拒绝考虑新材料，伊斯利克公司随即提出上诉。

在理解专利主张范围的过程中，地区法院排除了两个附加挂钩及其垂直排列作为功能性特征，但保留了挂钩形状、扩展的尖端、两端的球体以及90度偏移。法院发现有三处装饰性差异，从而得出初步结论，即普通观察者不会被欺骗。在上诉中，伊斯利克公司认为这是一个细节清单，而不是对整体视觉效果的评估。这个论点的问题是，地区法院明确表示它确实比较了“两种产品的整体视觉效果”。在上诉中，联邦巡回法院支持这一观点，认为考虑区分特征“不是法律错误”，并且“很难想象法院如何能够合理地进行这种分析，而不指出这些特征”。

上述图片是从地区法院的临时禁令裁决中复制的，左侧是该案中主张的D'526专利图，右侧是亚马逊上被指控的设备。该图片似乎是提交给法院的全部证据基础，显然不够充分。

四位知识产权教授——莎拉·法克瑞尔（Sarah Fackrell）、埃里克·高德曼（Eric Goldman）、伊丽莎白·罗森布拉特（Elizabeth Rosenblatt）和萨乌拉布·维什努巴卡特（Saurabh Vishnubhakat）——通过斯坦福大学的Juelsgaard诊所提交了一份友情陈述书，支持维持原判。法官引用教授们的说法，将“Schedule A”案件描述为“原告将大量无关的在线商贩合并为一起侵权诉讼”，并获得单方面法庭命令，“在被告未收到通知或无法质疑原告的指控之前”。不过，法官最终认为，关于“Schedule A”案件是否被允许或具有滥用性的问题并未被当事人适当提出。

虽然我同意上诉法院不必评议合并审理的问题，因为下级法院并未受到挑战，但这种情况可能永远不会上升到联邦巡回法院，因为其策略性使用针对的是通常不会出庭的外国实体（因此不会上诉）。在此案中，一名被告确实出庭，但在地区法院胜诉，因此没有对“Schedule A”设置提出上诉。
articles.summary:
by Dennis Crouch

The Federal Circuit has affirmed denial of preliminary injunction in the Schedule A design patent case of Jacki Easlick, LLC v. CJ Emerald, Nos. 2024-1538, -1826 (Fed. Cir. Aug. 14, 2026) (nonprecedential).I wrote about the pending case in June while the Range of Motion en banc petition was still pending.  Both of these are now closed.

The actual opinion here is lightweight — like the claimed handbag hangers.  It is non-precedential – essentially finding no abuse of discretion based upon a deferential standard review. The more interesting part of the opinion is where it highlights a set of questions, but then refuses to answer them.

  1. The court declined to address Schedule A practice, despite extensive amicus briefing.
  2. The court declined to engage with Chief Judge Moore’s concerns about the “plainly dissimilar” test.
  3. The court declined to address whether a core feature of the claimed purse hook—the ninety-degree orientation—is functional, explaining only that resolution of the issue “does not affect our analysis.”

I’ll note also that the opinion describes the law professors’ amicus brief as “arguing that so-called ‘Schedule A’ cases are legally permissible.”  This appears to be a big typo – because the brief argues the opposite – that they are legally impermissible.

Jacki Easlick owns U.S. Design Patent No. D695,526 on the TOTE HANGER, a two-part hook that holds a handbag perpendicular to a closet rod. This is the type of product that is easy to copy and sell via Amazon or other online storefront.  In 2023, Easlick sued 67 online sellers in a single complaint in the Western District of Pennsylvania and obtained a same-day ex parte temporary restraining order against all of them, including an asset freeze. AccEncyc, a China-based Amazon seller, appeared and contested infringement. The district court then denied a preliminary injunction based both on likelihood of success and irreparable harm. Easlick moved for reconsideration and offered the physical hooks it had not submitted the first time. The court refused to consider the new material and Easlick then appealed.

In its claim construction process, the district court excluded the two attached hooks and their vertical arrangement as functional, but kept the hook shapes, the flared tip, the spheres on the ends, and the ninety-degree offset. It then found three ornamental differences — leading the court to a (preliminary) conclusion that an ordinary observer would not be deceived. On appeal Easlick argued that this was a checklist of details rather than an assessment of overall visual impression.  The problem with this argument is that the district court stated that it did in fact compare “the overall visual effect of the two products.”  On appeal, the Federal Circuit bolstered this – finding that considering distinguishing features “is not legal error,” and that “it is hard to imagine how a court could reasonably conduct this analysis without pointing such features out.”

The image above – reproduced in the opinion from the district court’s preliminary injunction ruling has the D’526 drawings asserted in the case on the left and the  accused devices on the right from the Amazon.  That image was apparently the entire evidentiary basis presented to the court — not really enough.

Four intellectual property professors, Sarah Fackrell, Eric Goldman, Elizabeth Rosenblatt, and Saurabh Vishnubhakat, filed an amicus brief supporting affirmance through Stanford’s Juelsgaard Clinic.  The panel quotes the professors to describe  a Schedule A case as one where “a plaintiff joins together a large number of unrelated online merchants in a single infringement complaint” and obtains an ex parte order “before Appellee had notice or could contest Appellants’ allegations.” But, ultimately finds that the issue of whether Schedule A cases are permitted or abusive was not properly raised by the parties.

While I agree that the panel was not required to reach joinder since it was not challenged below, this is a situation that may never reach the Federal Circuit because its strategic use against foreign entities who typically never appear in court (and thus never appeal).  Here, one defendant did appear, but won at the district court and so did not appeal the Schedule A setup.
